newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Schering's Q1 97 profits rise 10-15 percent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Schering's Q1 97 profits rise 10-15 percent.

text.p: Shares in German pharmaceutical group Schering AG gained ground on Wednesday after its first quarter 1997 profits rose and it said that it planned to buy back large amounts of its own shares.
Schering said profits for the first quarter of 1997 had risen between 10 and 15 percent from a year earlier, while group sales were up 21 percent.
The firm also said the current dollar/mark exchange rate would boost profits for the whole year by around 10 to 15 percent.
The German share market reacted positively to the figures and news of the share buy-back, with Schering stock ending bourse trade up five marks at 166 marks.
"It seems to have triggered speculative buys," said Andreas Schmidt, chemicals analyst at BZW Deutschland, who has a 'buy' recommendation on Schering.
"The numbers themselves were nothing special, in fact just slightly below our expectations, but the share had also underperformed in the past few days and is catching up now."

Further positive news for the share price came later when Schering's board chairman Giuseppe Vita said he thought there was room to manoeuvre on a higher dividend pay-out in 1997, as currently only 30 percent of group profit was paid out in dividends.
The group paid a dividend of two marks per five mark share for 1996, up from 1.55 marks the previous year.
Schering said it planned the share buy-back when this became legally possible, in order to fend off any attempted takeovers or mergers of the company.
Legal restrictions currently make share buy-backs a near impossibility in Germany, except under emergency conditions.

A Schering spokesman said the company would buy back shares in several chunks to a value of around 500 million marks, ($289.4 million) but added that Schering did not see itself at risk of a hostile takeover attempt as it was "too expensive and too specialised."
He said Schering had a current market value of 11 billion marks and that a potential buyer would have to offer at least 16 billion marks.
Moreover, the firm's structure was so streamlined that "not even 5,000 people could be let go" after a takeover, he said.
Vita told the firm's annual meeting that the first three months of this year had developed very favourably due to the dollar/mark level.
The mark has weakened substantially against the dollar in recent months and was trading at 1.7336 in afternoon trade on Wednesday.
In 1996, Schering said its total sales were 5.27 billion marks -- a figure which Vita said would this year rise by 14 percent to around six billion marks.
Schering also said that its plant protection unit AgrEvo, which it operates with Hoechst AG, would continue to develop genetic technology and bio-techology.

"It is our ecological duty to use developments in the area of genetic technology," management board member Klaus Pohle said, as they could increase agricultural revenues and reduce the need for plant protection.
Pohle said that if Germany did not continue to develop genetic technology, it could fall behind other countries.

A London-based pharmaceuticals analyst, who did not wish to be named, said: "Schering is doing well because it is a very focused pharmaceutical company. You're also seeing the positive impact of the dollar."
-- Clifford Coonan, Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 7565 ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
